title: Developing Skills Through Job Rotation
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The piece takes on talent hoarding directly, starting from why it feels rational: leaders depend on star performers for the work that matters, so letting them move looks like a reliable way to undermine results. Its counter-argument is that protecting top performers produces the opposite of what the leader wants, undermining talent development and creating stagnation, with the cost landing on the wider organisation. Job rotation is then asserted in strong terms as the single most effective developmental mechanism available, on two grounds: people who take new roles under new leaders in different environments develop faster, and they are more likely to be retained over the long run. The retention argument is the one most likely to move a hoarding leader, since it reframes mobility as a way of keeping people rather than losing them. The essay is clear that the obstacle is interpersonal rather than procedural, requiring leaders to talk peers out of a fear of losing their go-to people, and it closes by putting the obligation on leaders themselves.
points: The counterintuitive claim is that protecting star performers produces stagnation and weaker development, so hoarding costs the leader the very capability they were guarding.
Job rotation is named as the single most effective developmental mechanism, not one option among several.
The retention argument is the one that answers the hoarder's real fear: people stay longer where their skills are aggressively invested in, so mobility keeps talent rather than losing it.
The named obstacle is interpersonal, requiring leaders to persuade peers out of protecting their go-to team members, which makes this a peer-negotiation problem rather than a policy one.
Development is framed as requiring a strategic commitment to a leadership pipeline, not as something that happens through goodwill.
quotes: The idea of willingly allowing these team members to work elsewhere within the team or organization seems like a surefire way of undermining results.
Holding top performers hostage to one area of a team or organization actually results in undermining talent development and creates stagnation.
When leaders protect talent and discourage talent mobility, the larger organization suffers.
Indisputably, nothing is as effective in developing leaders as job rotation.
Team members who take on new roles and assignments under new leaders, often in different environments, develop their leadership talents more quickly.
Better yet, team members tend to make a permanent home where their skills are aggressively invested in, especially through job rotation.
This means convincing some colleagues not to hoard and protect talent because of their fear of losing their go-to team members.
